topics.name: Rational Numbers
topics.summary: Understand rational numbers and find rationals between two numbers.

steps.title: Number families
steps.text: Natural numbers N = 1, 2, 3, … Whole numbers W add 0. Integers Z add negatives: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …

steps.title: What is a rational number?
steps.text: A number is rational if it can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Every integer is rational because n = n/1.

steps.title: Equivalent forms
steps.text: A rational number has many equal forms, like 1/2 = 2/4 = 5/10. We usually write it in lowest terms, where p and q have no common factor other than 1.

steps.title: Rationals between two numbers
steps.text: Between any two rational numbers there are infinitely many rationals. One way: take the average. Another: write both with a bigger common denominator and pick fractions in between.

steps.title: On the number line
steps.text: Every rational number has a point on the number line. Divide each unit into q equal parts and count p parts from 0.
steps.example: 3/4: split 0 to 1 into 4 parts, take the 3rd mark

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a rational number?
quiz.explanation: p/q needs q ≠ 0, so 5/0 is not defined and is not rational.

quiz.q: Which statement is true?
options: Every rational number is an integer
Every integer is a rational number
Every rational number is a natural number
quiz.explanation: Any integer n can be written as n/1, so it is rational. The reverse is not true (1/2 is not an integer).

quiz.q: A rational number between 1/3 and 1/2 is:
quiz.explanation: 1/3 ≈ 0.333, 1/2 = 0.5, and 2/5 = 0.4 lies between them.

quiz.q: Find five rational numbers between 3/5 and 4/5.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Multiply numerator and denominator by 12: 3/5 = 36/60 and 4/5 = 48/60.
Numbers between: 37/60, 38/60, 39/60, 40/60, 41/60.
Simplified: 37/60, 19/30, 13/20, 2/3, 41/60.
So five rationals are 37/60, 38/60, 39/60, 40/60, 41/60.

quiz.q: Is zero a rational number? Can you write it in p/q form?
quiz.modelAnswer:
Yes, 0 is a rational number.
It can be written as 0 = 0/1 = 0/2 = 0/(−5), where p = 0 and q is any non-zero integer.
Since p and q are integers with q ≠ 0, 0 fits the definition of a rational number.

topics.name: Irrational Numbers
topics.summary: Meet numbers like √2 and π that cannot be written as p/q.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.text: A number that cannot be written in the form p/q (p, q integers, q ≠ 0) is irrational. Pythagoreans discovered √2 is irrational.

steps.title: Square roots
steps.text: √n is irrational if n is a positive integer that is not a perfect square. If n is a perfect square, √n is a natural number.

steps.title: Real numbers
steps.text: Rational and irrational numbers together form the real numbers, R. Every real number has a unique point on the number line, and every point is a real number.

steps.title: Locating √2
steps.text: Draw a unit square on the number line from 0 to 1. Its diagonal is √(1² + 1²) = √2. With centre 0 and radius equal to the diagonal, draw an arc to cut the line.

steps.title: Square root spiral
steps.text: From √2, draw a perpendicular of length 1 and join to O. The new hypotenuse is √3. Repeating gives √4, √5, … one after another.

quiz.q: Which number is irrational?
quiz.explanation: 7 is not a perfect square, so √7 is irrational. √16 = 4 and 22/7 is a fraction.

quiz.q: π is:
quiz.explanation: π is irrational; 22/7 is only an approximate rational value.

quiz.q: In a square with side 1 unit, the diagonal is:
quiz.explanation: By Pythagoras, diagonal = √(1² + 1²) = √2.

quiz.q: Is √4 irrational? Justify. Give one example of the square root of a number which is rational.
quiz.modelAnswer:
No, √4 is not irrational.
√4 = 2 = 2/1, which is of the form p/q.
So √4 is rational.
Another example: √25 = 5 is also rational because 25 is a perfect square.

quiz.q: Show how √5 can be represented on the number line.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Mark O at 0 and A at 2 on the number line, so OA = 2.
At A draw AB ⊥ OA with AB = 1 unit.
By Pythagoras, OB = √(2² + 1²) = √5.
With centre O and radius OB, draw an arc cutting the number line at P.
Then P represents √5.

topics.name: Real Numbers and Decimal Expansions
topics.summary: Use decimal expansions to tell rational and irrational numbers apart.

steps.title: Terminating decimals
steps.text: Some rationals end after a few digits. This happens when the denominator (in lowest terms) has only 2s and 5s as prime factors.

steps.title: Non-terminating recurring
steps.text: Other rationals go on forever but a block of digits repeats. We show the repeating block with a bar.

steps.title: Irrational decimals
steps.text: An irrational number has a decimal expansion that is non-terminating and non-recurring. No block repeats forever.

steps.title: Recurring decimal to p/q
steps.text: Let x equal the decimal. Multiply by 10, 100, … so the repeating part lines up, then subtract to remove it.

steps.title: Finding an irrational between numbers
steps.text: Write a non-terminating, non-repeating decimal between the two numbers.

quiz.q: The decimal expansion of 3/8 is:
quiz.explanation: 8 = 2³ has only the prime 2, so 3/8 = 0.375 terminates.

quiz.q: 0.4̅ in p/q form is:
Which decimal represents an irrational number?
quiz.explanation: 0.1010010001… never ends and never repeats a fixed block, so it is irrational.

quiz.q: Express 0.47̅ (that is, 0.4777…) in the form p/q.
Write the decimal expansion of 1/7 and state its type. Without dividing, can you predict 2/7?
quiz.modelAnswer:
1/7 = 0.142857142857… = 0.142857̅, which is non-terminating recurring.
2/7 = 2 × 0.142857̅ = 0.285714̅.
The same six digits repeat in a shifted order.

topics.name: Operations on Real Numbers
topics.summary: Add, multiply and rationalise expressions with square roots.

steps.title: Rational with irrational
steps.text: Rational + irrational is irrational. Rational (non-zero) × irrational is irrational. But irrational + irrational may be rational or irrational.

steps.title: Useful identities
steps.text: For positive a, b: √(ab) = √a·√b and √(a/b) = √a/√b. Also (√a + √b)(√a − √b) = a − b and (√a + √b)² = a + 2√(ab) + b.

steps.title: Like surds
steps.text: You can add only like surds, just like like terms in algebra.

steps.title: Rationalising
steps.text: To remove a root from the denominator, multiply top and bottom by a suitable factor. For a + √b, use its conjugate a − √b.

steps.title: Conjugate example
steps.text: Multiplying by the conjugate makes the denominator rational using (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².

quiz.q: Rationalising 1/√7 gives:
quiz.explanation: Multiply by √7/√7: √7/7.

quiz.q: Which is irrational?
quiz.explanation: (√2)² = 2, √36 = 6, and 0 are rational; rational + irrational (3 + √5) is irrational.

quiz.q: Rationalise the denominator of 1/(√7 − 2).
quiz.modelAnswer:
Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate √7 + 2:
1/(√7 − 2) × (√7 + 2)/(√7 + 2)
= (√7 + 2)/((√7)² − 2²)
= (√7 + 2)/(7 − 4)
= (√7 + 2)/3.

quiz.q: Simplify (√5 + √2)².

topics.name: Laws of Exponents for Real Numbers
topics.summary: Apply exponent laws to powers with rational exponents.

steps.title: Basic laws
steps.text: For a > 0 and rational p, q: aᵖ·a^q = a^(p+q), (aᵖ)^q = a^(pq), aᵖ/a^q = a^(p−q), and aᵖ·bᵖ = (ab)ᵖ.

steps.title: Zero and negative powers
steps.text: Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1. A negative power means the reciprocal.

steps.title: nth roots
steps.text: For a > 0, the nth root ⁿ√a = a^(1/n). It is the positive number which, raised to n, gives a.

steps.title: Rational exponents
steps.text: a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)^m = ⁿ√(a^m). Take the root first to keep numbers small.

steps.title: Combining
steps.text: Write numbers as powers of primes, then apply the laws step by step.

quiz.q: 64^(1/2) equals:

quiz.explanation: Add the powers: 2/3 + 1/3 = 1, so the answer is 2¹ = 2.

quiz.q: Find the value of 16^(3/4).

topics.name: Polynomials in One Variable
topics.summary: Learn terms, coefficients, degree and types of polynomials.

steps.title: What is a polynomial?
steps.text: An algebraic expression whose variable has only whole-number powers is a polynomial. Each part joined by + or − is a term; the number with it is the coefficient.

steps.title: Not a polynomial
steps.text: If the variable has a negative or fractional power, the expression is not a polynomial.

steps.title: Degree
steps.text: The highest power of the variable is the degree. A non-zero constant has degree 0. The degree of the zero polynomial is not defined.

steps.title: Types by terms
steps.text: Monomial: 1 term. Binomial: 2 terms. Trinomial: 3 terms.

steps.title: Types by degree
steps.text: Degree 1: linear. Degree 2: quadratic. Degree 3: cubic. A linear polynomial in x looks like ax + b, a ≠ 0.

quiz.q: Which is a polynomial in one variable?
quiz.explanation: Only 4x² − 3x + 7 has whole-number powers of a single variable.

quiz.q: Degree of 5t − √7 is:
quiz.explanation: The highest power of t is 1, so it is linear (degree 1).

quiz.q: x³ + x is a:
quiz.explanation: Two terms (binomial) and highest power 3 (cubic).

quiz.q: Write the coefficient of x² in (i) 2 + x² + x  (ii) 2 − x² + x³  (iii) (π/2)x² + x.
quiz.modelAnswer:
(i) In 2 + x² + x, the coefficient of x² is 1.
(ii) In 2 − x² + x³, the coefficient of x² is −1.
(iii) In (π/2)x² + x, the coefficient of x² is π/2.

quiz.q: Give one example each of a binomial of degree 35 and a monomial of degree 100.
quiz.modelAnswer:
A binomial has two terms; highest power 35: x³⁵ + 1 (or x³⁵ − x).
A monomial has one term; power 100: 2y¹⁰⁰ (or y¹⁰⁰).

topics.name: Zeroes of a Polynomial
topics.summary: Find values of p(x) and the zeroes of a polynomial.

steps.title: Value of a polynomial
steps.text: Replace x by a number and calculate. The result p(c) is the value of p(x) at x = c.

steps.title: Zero of a polynomial
steps.text: A number c is a zero of p(x) if p(c) = 0. Finding a zero is the same as solving p(x) = 0.

steps.title: Linear polynomial
steps.text: ax + b (a ≠ 0) has exactly one zero, x = −b/a.

steps.title: Many or no zeroes
steps.text: A non-zero constant polynomial has no zero. Every real number is a zero of the zero polynomial. A polynomial can have more than one zero.

quiz.q: The zero of p(x) = 3x − 6 is:
quiz.explanation: 3x − 6 = 0 gives x = 2.

quiz.q: If p(x) = x² − 2x + 1, then p(1) is:
quiz.explanation: 1 − 2 + 1 = 0, so 1 is a zero.

quiz.q: The zero of p(x) = cx + d (c ≠ 0) is:
quiz.explanation: cx + d = 0 gives x = −d/c.

quiz.q: Find p(0), p(1) and p(2) for p(y) = y² − y + 1.
Verify whether 1 and −1 are zeroes of p(x) = x² − 1, then find the zero of p(x) = 2x + 1.
quiz.modelAnswer:
p(1) = 1² − 1 = 0, so 1 is a zero.
p(−1) = (−1)² − 1 = 0, so −1 is a zero.
For 2x + 1 = 0, 2x = −1, so x = −1/2 is the zero.

topics.name: Factorisation of Polynomials
topics.summary: Use the Factor Theorem and splitting the middle term to factorise.

steps.title: Factor Theorem
steps.text: If p(x) has degree ≥ 1 and a is a real number: (x − a) is a factor of p(x) if p(a) = 0, and if (x − a) is a factor then p(a) = 0.
steps.example: p(x) = x² − 5x + 6, p(2) = 0 → (x − 2) is a factor

steps.title: Checking a factor
steps.text: To test (x + a), find p(−a). If it is 0, (x + a) is a factor.
steps.example: x³ + 1: p(−1) = 0, so (x + 1) is a factor

steps.title: Splitting the middle term
steps.text: For ax² + bx + c, find two numbers p and q with p + q = b and pq = ac. Split bx and group.

steps.title: Factorising cubics
steps.text: Find one zero a by trying factors of the constant term. Then (x − a) is a factor; divide or compare to get a quadratic and factorise it.

quiz.q: Is (x − 1) a factor of x³ − 1?
quiz.explanation: p(1) = 1 − 1 = 0, so by the Factor Theorem (x − 1) is a factor.

quiz.q: x² − 5x + 6 factorises as:
quiz.explanation: Numbers with sum −5 and product 6 are −2 and −3.

quiz.q: If (x − 2) is a factor of x² + kx + 2, then k equals:
Factorise 12x² − 7x + 1.
Factorise x³ − 2x² − x + 2.

topics.name: Algebraic Identities
topics.summary: Use standard identities to expand, factorise and evaluate quickly.

steps.title: Square identities
steps.text: (x + y)² = x² + 2xy + y² and (x − y)² = x² − 2xy + y². Also x² − y² = (x + y)(x − y).

steps.title: Product identity
steps.text: (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab.

steps.title: Square of a trinomial
steps.text: (x + y + z)² = x² + y² + z² + 2xy + 2yz + 2zx.

steps.title: Cube identities
steps.text: (x + y)³ = x³ + y³ + 3xy(x + y) and (x − y)³ = x³ − y³ − 3xy(x − y).

steps.title: Sum of cubes rule
steps.text: x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz = (x + y + z)(x² + y² + z² − xy − yz − zx). So if x + y + z = 0, then x³ + y³ + z³ = 3xyz.

quiz.q: (x + 4)(x + 10) equals:
quiz.explanation: (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab = x² + 14x + 40.

quiz.q: 99² equals:
If a + b + c = 0, then a³ + b³ + c³ equals:
quiz.explanation: From x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz = (x + y + z)(…), with sum 0 we get a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc.

quiz.q: Evaluate 105 × 106 using a suitable identity.
Factorise 8x³ + 27y³ + 36x²y + 54xy².
quiz.modelAnswer:
8x³ = (2x)³ and 27y³ = (3y)³.
3(2x)²(3y) = 36x²y and 3(2x)(3y)² = 54xy².
So the expression = (2x)³ + (3y)³ + 3(2x)(3y)(2x + 3y) = (2x + 3y)³
= (2x + 3y)(2x + 3y)(2x + 3y).

topics.name: Cartesian System
topics.summary: Learn the axes, origin and quadrants of the coordinate plane.

steps.title: Why coordinates?
steps.text: To fix the position of a point on a plane, we need two references. Descartes used two perpendicular lines for this.
steps.example: Like a seat: row and column

steps.title: The axes
steps.text: The horizontal number line is the x-axis (XX′) and the vertical one is the y-axis (YY′). They meet at the origin O.

steps.title: Positive and negative
steps.text: On the x-axis, right of O is positive and left is negative. On the y-axis, above O is positive and below is negative.
steps.example: OX and OY are positive directions

steps.title: Four quadrants
steps.text: The axes divide the plane into four quadrants, numbered anticlockwise from the top right: I, II, III, IV.

quiz.q: The point where the x-axis and y-axis meet is called:
quiz.explanation: The axes intersect at the origin, (0, 0).

quiz.q: The two axes are:
quiz.explanation: In the Cartesian system the x-axis and y-axis are perpendicular.

quiz.q: Quadrant II has signs:
quiz.explanation: In quadrant II, x is negative and y is positive.

quiz.q: Name the axes and the parts into which they divide the plane. Write the sign of coordinates in each part.
quiz.modelAnswer:
The horizontal line is the x-axis and the vertical line is the y-axis; they meet at the origin.
They divide the plane into four quadrants:
I: (+, +), II: (−, +), III: (−, −), IV: (+, −).

quiz.q: Why do we need two numbers to fix the position of a point on a plane? Give an example.
quiz.modelAnswer:
One number can only give a position along a line.
A plane has two directions, so we need a distance along the horizontal and one along the vertical.
Example: a lamp is 5 m from one wall and 3 m from the other wall; both values are needed to locate it.

topics.name: Coordinates of a Point
topics.summary: Read and write the abscissa and ordinate of any point.

steps.title: x-coordinate
steps.text: The perpendicular distance of a point from the y-axis, measured along the x-axis, is its x-coordinate or abscissa.

steps.title: y-coordinate
steps.text: The perpendicular distance from the x-axis, measured along the y-axis, is the y-coordinate or ordinate.

steps.title: Writing coordinates
steps.text: Write (x, y): x first, then y. Order matters, so (3, 4) and (4, 3) are different points.

steps.title: Points on the axes
steps.text: A point on the x-axis has y = 0, like (a, 0). A point on the y-axis has x = 0, like (0, b). Points on axes are in no quadrant.

quiz.q: The abscissa of (−7, 2) is:
quiz.explanation: The abscissa is the x-coordinate, −7.

quiz.q: The point (0, −4) lies:
quiz.explanation: x = 0, so it lies on the y-axis.

quiz.q: In which quadrant does (3, −5) lie?
quiz.explanation: x positive, y negative → quadrant IV.

quiz.q: Write the quadrant or axis for each point: (−2, 4), (3, −1), (−1, 0), (1, 2), (−3, −5).
quiz.modelAnswer:
(−2, 4): x < 0, y > 0 → quadrant II.
(3, −1): x > 0, y < 0 → quadrant IV.
(−1, 0): y = 0 → on the negative x-axis.
(1, 2): quadrant I.
(−3, −5): quadrant III.

quiz.q: A point lies on the x-axis at a distance of 5 units to the left of the origin. Write its coordinates, abscissa and ordinate.
quiz.modelAnswer:
On the x-axis, y = 0.
Left of the origin means x is negative, so x = −5.
Coordinates: (−5, 0).
Abscissa = −5, ordinate = 0.

topics.name: Plotting Points in the Plane
topics.summary: Plot given points step by step on graph paper.

steps.title: Choose a scale
steps.text: Draw the axes on graph paper and mark equal units on both. Usually 1 cm = 1 unit.

steps.title: Move along x
steps.text: From O, move along the x-axis by the x-coordinate: right if positive, left if negative.

steps.title: Move along y
steps.text: From there, move parallel to the y-axis by the y-coordinate: up if positive, down if negative. Mark the point.

steps.title: Mirror points
steps.text: (x, y) and (x, −y) are mirror images in the x-axis. (x, y) and (−x, y) are mirror images in the y-axis.

quiz.q: To plot (−4, −1), from O you move:
quiz.explanation: x = −4 means 4 left; y = −1 means 1 down.

quiz.q: If x = y for a point, which point could it be?
quiz.explanation: Only (5, 5) has equal coordinates.

quiz.q: The mirror image of (4, 7) in the x-axis is:
quiz.explanation: Reflecting in the x-axis changes the sign of y.

quiz.q: Plot A(2, 3), B(−2, 3), C(−2, −3) and D(2, −3). What figure is ABCD? Find its perimeter.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Plot each point by moving along x and then y.
AB = 4, BC = 6, CD = 4, DA = 6 units, with all angles 90°.
So ABCD is a rectangle.
Perimeter = 2(4 + 6) = 20 units.

quiz.q: Describe how to plot the point (3, −4) and name its quadrant.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Start at origin O.
Move 3 units right along the x-axis (x = 3 is positive).
Then move 4 units down parallel to the y-axis (y = −4).
Mark the point; it lies in quadrant IV.

topics.name: Linear Equations Revisited
topics.summary: Recall linear equations in one variable and their solutions.

steps.title: One-variable equations
steps.text: An equation like ax + b = 0 (a ≠ 0) is a linear equation in one variable. It has exactly one solution.

steps.title: Solving
steps.text: Do the same operation on both sides to keep the balance until x is alone.

steps.title: Checking
steps.text: Put the answer back into the equation. If both sides are equal, it is correct.

steps.title: Moving to two variables
steps.text: When a situation has two unknown quantities, we use two variables like x and y.
steps.example: Cost of pen x + cost of book y = ₹60

quiz.q: The solution of 5x − 10 = 0 is:
How many solutions does 4x + 3 = 0 have?
quiz.explanation: A linear equation in one variable has exactly one solution, x = −3/4.

quiz.q: Which is a linear equation in one variable?
quiz.explanation: Only 7x − 2 = 12 has one variable with power 1.

quiz.q: Solve 2(x + 3) = x − 4 and check your answer.
The cost of a notebook is twice the cost of a pen. Write this as an equation using two variables.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Let the cost of a notebook be ₹x and the cost of a pen be ₹y.
Notebook = 2 × pen, so x = 2y.
In standard form: x − 2y = 0.

topics.name: Linear Equations in Two Variables
topics.summary: Write equations in the form ax + by + c = 0 and identify a, b, c.

steps.title: Definition
steps.text: An equation that can be written as ax + by + c = 0, where a, b, c are real numbers and a, b are not both zero, is a linear equation in two variables.

steps.title: Standard form
steps.text: Move all terms to one side so the right side is 0. Then read a, b and c with their signs.

steps.title: Missing variable
steps.text: An equation like x = −5 can also be seen in two variables: 1·x + 0·y + 5 = 0.

steps.title: Word problems
steps.text: Name the unknowns as x and y, then turn the sentence into an equation.
steps.example: Runs by two batsmen total 176: x + y = 176

quiz.q: In 3x − 4y = 7, the value of c in ax + by + c = 0 is:
x = 6 in the form ax + by + c = 0 is:
quiz.explanation: There is no y-term, so b = 0: 1·x + 0·y − 6 = 0.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a linear equation in two variables?
quiz.explanation: x² has power 2, so x² + y = 3 is not linear.

quiz.q: Write −2x + 3y = 6 and x = 3y in the form ax + by + c = 0 and state a, b, c for each.
The cost of a notebook is ₹x and a pen is ₹y. 3 notebooks and 2 pens cost ₹100. Write the linear equation and its standard form.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Cost of 3 notebooks = 3x, cost of 2 pens = 2y.
Total: 3x + 2y = 100.
Standard form: 3x + 2y − 100 = 0, with a = 3, b = 2, c = −100.

topics.name: Solutions of a Linear Equation
topics.summary: Find solutions (x, y) and see why there are infinitely many.

steps.title: What is a solution?
steps.text: A pair of values (x, y) that makes both sides equal is a solution. Write it as an ordered pair.

steps.title: Finding solutions
steps.text: Choose any value of x, put it in the equation and solve for y. Easy choices are x = 0 and y = 0.

steps.title: Infinitely many
steps.text: Since x can be any real number, a linear equation in two variables has infinitely many solutions.

steps.title: Checking a pair
steps.text: Substitute both values. If LHS = RHS, the pair is a solution; otherwise it is not.
steps.example: Is (1, 1) a solution of x + 2y = 6? 1 + 2 = 3 ≠ 6, so no

quiz.q: How many solutions does 2x + 5y = 10 have?
quiz.explanation: Each x gives a y, so there are infinitely many solutions.

quiz.q: Which pair is a solution of x − 2y = 4?
If (2, k) is a solution of 2x + 3y = 13, then k is:
Find four different solutions of 2x + y = 7.
Check whether (0, 2), (√2, 4√2) and (1, 1) are solutions of x − 2y = 4.
quiz.modelAnswer:
For (0, 2): 0 − 2(2) = −4 ≠ 4, so not a solution.
For (√2, 4√2): √2 − 8√2 = −7√2 ≠ 4, so not a solution.
For (1, 1): 1 − 2 = −1 ≠ 4, so not a solution.
None of these pairs satisfy x − 2y = 4.

topics.name: Euclid's Definitions
topics.summary: Know how Euclid defined point, line and surface.

steps.title: Origins of geometry
steps.text: Geometry means 'earth measurement'. Egyptians and Indians used it for land and altars. Around 300 BCE, Euclid collected it in a book called 'Elements'.

steps.title: Point and line
steps.text: A point is that which has no part. A line is breadthless length. The ends of a line are points.
steps.example: A dot on paper models a point

steps.title: Straight line and surface
steps.text: A straight line lies evenly with the points on itself. A surface has length and breadth only. The edges of a surface are lines.
steps.example: The top of a table models a surface

steps.title: Undefined terms
steps.text: Euclid's definitions use other words like 'part', 'breadth' and 'length' that are not defined. So today point, line and plane are taken as undefined terms.

steps.title: Solids
steps.text: A solid has shape, size, position and three dimensions. Boundaries of solids are surfaces, boundaries of surfaces are curves, and ends of curves are points.

quiz.q: Euclid's book of geometry is called:
quiz.explanation: Euclid compiled geometry in 'Elements', with 13 books.

quiz.q: According to Euclid, 'a point is that which has':
quiz.explanation: Euclid's first definition: a point is that which has no part.

quiz.q: How many dimensions does a surface have?
quiz.explanation: A surface has length and breadth, so 2 dimensions.

quiz.q: Why are point, line and plane taken as undefined terms?
quiz.modelAnswer:
Euclid defined a point as 'that which has no part' and a line as 'breadthless length'.
These definitions use words like part, breadth and length which themselves need definitions.
This leads to an endless chain of definitions.
So mathematicians agree to leave point, line and plane undefined.

quiz.q: Write the dimensions of a solid, a surface, a line and a point, with one example each.
quiz.modelAnswer:
A solid has 3 dimensions, e.g. a cube.
A surface has 2 dimensions, e.g. a sheet of paper.
A line has 1 dimension, e.g. the edge of a ruler.
A point has 0 dimensions, e.g. a dot.

topics.name: Euclid's Axioms
topics.summary: Use Euclid's axioms (common notions) in reasoning.

steps.title: Axioms
steps.text: Axioms are assumptions used throughout mathematics, not only in geometry. They are accepted as obvious truths without proof.

steps.title: Equals with equals
steps.text: (1) Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another. (2) If equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal. (3) If equals are subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal.
steps.example: a = c and b = c ⇒ a = b

steps.title: Coincide and whole
steps.text: (4) Things which coincide with one another are equal. (5) The whole is greater than the part.

steps.title: Halves and doubles
steps.text: (6) Things which are double of the same things are equal. (7) Things which are halves of the same things are equal.

steps.title: Using axioms
steps.text: Axioms let us make statements without measuring. Every step in a proof should rest on an axiom, postulate, definition or proved result.
steps.example: AB = BC, BC = CD ⇒ AB = CD (Axiom 1)

quiz.q: If a = b and b = c, then a = c. This uses Euclid's axiom:
options: The whole is greater than the part
Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another
quiz.explanation: Both a and c equal b, so they are equal to each other (Axiom 1).

quiz.q: 'The whole is greater than the part' is:
quiz.explanation: It is Euclid's 5th axiom (common notion).

quiz.q: If x + y = 10 and x = z, then z + y = 10 uses which idea?
options: A straight line can be drawn
quiz.explanation: Adding y to the equals x and z gives equal wholes.

quiz.q: Ram and Shyam have the same weight. If each gains 2 kg, how will their new weights compare? State the axiom used.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Let each weigh w kg. After gaining 2 kg each, both weigh (w + 2) kg.
So their new weights are equal.
Axiom used: If equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal (Axiom 2).

quiz.q: In the figure, AC = BD. Show that AB = CD, where A, B, C, D lie on a line in that order.
quiz.modelAnswer:
AC = AB + BC and BD = BC + CD (point B lies between A and C; C between B and D).
Given AC = BD, so AB + BC = BC + CD.
Subtracting BC from both sides (equals subtracted from equals give equal remainders, Axiom 3):
AB = CD.

topics.name: Euclid's Postulates
topics.summary: Learn Euclid's five postulates and the meaning of the fifth.

steps.title: Postulates
steps.text: Postulates are assumptions specific to geometry. Euclid gave five of them.

steps.title: Postulates 1 to 3
steps.text: (1) A straight line may be drawn from any one point to any other point. (2) A terminated line can be produced indefinitely. (3) A circle can be drawn with any centre and any radius.
steps.example: Through two distinct points, exactly one line passes

steps.title: Postulate 4
steps.text: All right angles are equal to one another.

steps.title: Postulate 5
steps.text: If a line falling on two straight lines makes the interior angles on the same side less than two right angles, the two lines, if produced, meet on that side.

steps.title: Theorems and consistency
steps.text: Statements proved using axioms and postulates are theorems. A system of axioms is consistent if no statement and its opposite can both be proved.
steps.example: Two distinct lines cannot have more than one point in common

quiz.q: How many postulates did Euclid give?
quiz.explanation: Euclid stated five postulates.

quiz.q: 'All right angles are equal to one another' is Euclid's:
quiz.explanation: This is Euclid's fourth postulate.

quiz.q: Number of lines passing through two distinct points:
quiz.explanation: A unique line passes through two distinct points (based on Postulate 1).

quiz.q: Prove that two distinct lines cannot have more than one point in common.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Suppose two distinct lines l and m have two common points P and Q.
Then both l and m pass through P and Q.
But only one line can pass through two distinct points (Postulate 1).
This contradicts that l and m are distinct.
Hence two distinct lines can have at most one point in common.

quiz.q: State Euclid's fifth postulate and explain it in simple words.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Fifth postulate: If a straight line falling on two straight lines makes the interior angles on the same side together less than two right angles, then the two lines, if produced indefinitely, meet on that side.
In simple words: if ∠1 + ∠2 < 180° on one side, the lines lean towards each other and will meet on that side.
If the sum is exactly 180°, the lines never meet; they are parallel.

topics.name: Basic Terms and Types of Angles
topics.summary: Recall line, ray, segment and types of angles.

steps.title: Line, segment, ray
steps.text: A line extends both ways without end. A line segment has two end points. A ray has one end point and goes on in one direction.
steps.example: Line AB, segment AB, ray AB

steps.title: Collinear points
steps.text: Three or more points on the same line are collinear; otherwise they are non-collinear.
steps.example: A, B, C on one line → collinear

steps.title: Angle
steps.text: An angle is formed when two rays start from the same end point. The rays are its arms and the end point is its vertex.

steps.title: Types of angles
steps.text: Acute: between 0° and 90°. Right: 90°. Obtuse: between 90° and 180°. Straight: 180°. Reflex: between 180° and 360°.

steps.title: Complementary and supplementary
steps.text: Two angles are complementary if their sum is 90°, and supplementary if their sum is 180°. Adjacent angles share a vertex and an arm, with no common interior.

quiz.q: An angle of 150° is:
quiz.explanation: 150° is between 90° and 180°, so it is obtuse.

quiz.q: The complement of 62° is:
The supplement of 75° is:
Two supplementary angles differ by 40°. Find the angles.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Let the angles be x and x + 40°.
x + (x + 40°) = 180°
2x = 140°, so x = 70°.
The angles are 70° and 110°.

quiz.q: An angle is equal to its complement. Find it, and say what kind of angle it is.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Let the angle be x; its complement is 90° − x.
x = 90° − x
2x = 90°, so x = 45°.
45° is an acute angle.

topics.name: Pairs of Angles and Intersecting Lines
topics.summary: Use linear pairs and vertically opposite angles to find unknown angles.

steps.title: Linear pair
steps.text: If the non-common arms of two adjacent angles form a straight line, they form a linear pair. Their sum is 180°.

steps.title: Linear Pair Axiom
steps.text: If a ray stands on a line, the two adjacent angles add up to 180°. Conversely, if two adjacent angles add to 180°, their non-common arms form a line.

steps.title: Vertically opposite angles
steps.text: When two lines intersect, four angles form. Opposite angles are called vertically opposite angles.
steps.example: AB and CD meet at O: ∠AOC and ∠BOD

steps.title: Theorem 6.1
steps.text: If two lines intersect, the vertically opposite angles are equal. Proof: ∠AOC + ∠AOD = 180° and ∠AOD + ∠BOD = 180°, so ∠AOC = ∠BOD.

steps.title: Angles at a point
steps.text: Angles around a point add up to 360°. Use this with linear pairs to find unknowns.
steps.example: Four angles x, 2x, 3x, 4x at a point: 10x = 360°, x = 36°

quiz.q: Two lines intersect and one angle is 50°. The vertically opposite angle is:
quiz.explanation: Vertically opposite angles are equal, so it is 50°.

quiz.q: If two angles form a linear pair and one is 65°, the other is:
quiz.explanation: Linear pair sums to 180°: 180° − 65° = 115°.

quiz.q: In a linear pair, if the angles are x and 2x, then x is:
Lines AB and CD intersect at O. If ∠AOC + ∠BOE = 70° and ∠BOD = 40°, find ∠BOE and reflex ∠COE. (Ray OE lies between rays OC and OB, above line AB.)
quiz.modelAnswer:
∠AOC = ∠BOD = 40° (vertically opposite).
So ∠BOE = 70° − 40° = 30°.
On line AB: ∠AOC + ∠COE + ∠BOE = 180°, so ∠COE = 180° − 70° = 110°.
Reflex ∠COE = 360° − 110° = 250°.

quiz.q: Prove that if two lines intersect, the vertically opposite angles are equal.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Let lines AB and CD intersect at O.
Ray OA stands on line CD, so ∠AOC + ∠AOD = 180° (linear pair).
Ray OD stands on line AB, so ∠AOD + ∠BOD = 180°.
So ∠AOC + ∠AOD = ∠AOD + ∠BOD, giving ∠AOC = ∠BOD.
Similarly ∠AOD = ∠BOC.

topics.name: Parallel Lines and a Transversal
topics.summary: Identify angle pairs made by a transversal and use them with parallel lines.

steps.title: Transversal
steps.text: A line that cuts two or more lines at distinct points is a transversal. With two lines it makes 8 angles.
steps.example: Line l cuts m and n

steps.title: Angle pairs
steps.text: Corresponding angles: same position at each crossing. Alternate interior angles: inside, on opposite sides of the transversal. Interior angles on the same side: inside, on the same side.

steps.title: Corresponding Angles Axiom
steps.text: If a transversal cuts two parallel lines, each pair of corresponding angles is equal. Conversely, if corresponding angles are equal, the lines are parallel.

steps.title: Alternate interior angles
steps.text: If a transversal cuts two parallel lines, alternate interior angles are equal (Theorem 6.2). If alternate interior angles are equal, the lines are parallel.

steps.title: Co-interior angles
steps.text: If a transversal cuts two parallel lines, interior angles on the same side add up to 180° (Theorem 6.4). The converse is also true.

quiz.q: If two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, alternate interior angles are:
quiz.explanation: Alternate interior angles are equal when lines are parallel.

quiz.q: Interior angles on the same side of a transversal cutting two parallel lines add up to:
quiz.explanation: Co-interior angles are supplementary: 180°.

quiz.q: One co-interior angle is 3x and the other is 2x, with parallel lines. x =
AB ∥ CD and a transversal cuts them. One angle of a pair of interior angles on the same side is 115°. Find the other, and its corresponding angle pair.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Interior angles on the same side add to 180° (AB ∥ CD).
Other angle = 180° − 115° = 65°.
The angle corresponding to it at the other line is also 65° (corresponding angles axiom).

quiz.q: If a transversal cuts two lines such that alternate interior angles are equal, prove the lines are parallel.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Let transversal t cut lines l and m at P and Q, with alternate interior angles ∠3 (at P) = ∠5 (at Q).
At P, ∠1 is vertically opposite to ∠3, so ∠1 = ∠3.
Hence ∠1 = ∠5, and ∠1, ∠5 are corresponding angles.
By the converse of the corresponding angles axiom, l ∥ m.

topics.name: Lines Parallel to the Same Line
topics.summary: Prove and use: lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other.

steps.title: The idea
steps.text: If line m ∥ l and line n ∥ l, then m ∥ n. Lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other (Theorem 6.6).
steps.example: Railway tracks and a guide line

steps.title: Why it works
steps.text: Draw a transversal t across l, m and n. Since m ∥ l, ∠1 = ∠2 (corresponding). Since n ∥ l, ∠1 = ∠3. So ∠2 = ∠3.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: ∠2 and ∠3 are corresponding angles for lines m and n. Since they are equal, m ∥ n by the converse of the corresponding angles axiom.

steps.title: Solving problems
steps.text: Through a bend point, draw a line parallel to the given parallel lines. Then use alternate or co-interior angles.
steps.example: AB ∥ CD; draw EF ∥ AB through the bend

quiz.q: If l ∥ m and m ∥ n, then:
quiz.explanation: Lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other.

quiz.q: Lines m and n are both parallel to l. A transversal makes 70° with l at a corresponding position. The corresponding angle with n is:
quiz.explanation: Corresponding angles with parallel lines are equal, so 70°.

quiz.q: AB ∥ CD and CD ∥ EF. A transversal makes a 50° interior angle with AB. The alternate interior angle it makes with EF is:
quiz.explanation: AB ∥ EF, so alternate interior angles are equal: 50°.

quiz.q: AB ∥ CD and point E lies between the two lines. B is on AB and D is on CD, with ∠ABE = 45° and ∠EDC = 30° (both angles open towards E). Find ∠BED.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Through E draw EF ∥ AB. Since AB ∥ CD, EF ∥ CD too (lines parallel to the same line).
∠BEF = ∠ABE = 45° (alternate interior angles, AB ∥ EF).
∠FED = ∠EDC = 30° (alternate interior angles, EF ∥ CD).
∠BED = 45° + 30° = 75°.

quiz.q: Prove that two lines which are both parallel to a third line are parallel to each other.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Let m ∥ l and n ∥ l. Draw transversal t cutting l, m, n.
∠1 (with l) = ∠2 (with m) as corresponding angles, since m ∥ l.
∠1 = ∠3 (with n) as corresponding angles, since n ∥ l.
So ∠2 = ∠3, which are corresponding angles for m and n.
By the converse of the corresponding angles axiom, m ∥ n.

topics.name: Congruence of Triangles
topics.summary: Understand what makes two triangles congruent and how to match their parts.

steps.title: What is congruence?
steps.text: Two figures are congruent if they have exactly the same shape and size. If you place one on the other, they cover each other completely.
steps.example: Two ₹1 coins of the same type are congruent.

steps.title: Congruent triangles
steps.text: Two triangles are congruent if their three sides and three angles are equal to the matching sides and angles of the other.
steps.example: △ABC ≅ △PQR means AB = PQ, BC = QR, CA = RP and ∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q, ∠C = ∠R

steps.title: Order of letters matters
steps.text: In △ABC ≅ △PQR, A matches P, B matches Q and C matches R. Writing the vertices in the correct order shows which parts correspond.
steps.example: △ABC ≅ △PQR is not the same claim as △ABC ≅ △QRP

steps.title: CPCT
steps.text: Once two triangles are proved congruent, all their other matching parts are equal. We write this reason as CPCT: Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles.

quiz.q: If △ABC ≅ △PQR, which side is equal to BC?
quiz.explanation: B matches Q and C matches R, so BC = QR.

quiz.q: What does CPCT stand for?
quiz.explanation: CPCT = Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles.

quiz.q: If △DEF ≅ △XYZ, then ∠F equals:
quiz.explanation: F is the third letter, so it matches Z, the third letter.

quiz.q: △ABC ≅ △LMN. Write all six pairs of equal parts.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Matching vertices in order: A↔L, B↔M, C↔N.
Sides: AB = LM, BC = MN, CA = NL.
Angles: ∠A = ∠L, ∠B = ∠M, ∠C = ∠N.
All of these follow from CPCT.

quiz.q: Explain why two triangles with equal angles need not be congruent.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Congruent triangles must have the same shape and the same size.
Equal angles only make the shape the same.
For example, an equilateral triangle of side 2 cm and one of side 5 cm both have all angles 60°.
Their sides are different, so they are not congruent.

topics.name: SAS and ASA Congruence Rules
topics.summary: Use the SAS and ASA rules to prove triangles congruent.

steps.title: Why we need rules
steps.text: We don't need to check all six parts. Three well-chosen parts are enough to prove two triangles congruent.

steps.title: SAS rule
steps.text: If two sides and the angle included between them in one triangle are equal to two sides and the included angle of another, the triangles are congruent. The angle must lie between the two sides.

steps.title: ASA rule
steps.text: If two angles and the side included between them are equal to the matching two angles and included side of another triangle, the triangles are congruent.

steps.title: AAS rule
steps.text: If two angles are equal, the third angles are also equal (angle sum is 180°). So two angles and any one matching side also give congruence.

steps.title: Writing a proof
steps.text: List the three equal parts with reasons (given, common side, vertically opposite angles, alternate angles). Then name the rule and use CPCT for more results.

quiz.q: In SAS, the angle must be:
options: The angle opposite a given side
The angle included between the two sides
quiz.explanation: SAS needs the angle between the two given sides.

quiz.q: In △ABC and △DEF, ∠A = ∠D, AB = DE, ∠B = ∠E. Which rule proves congruence?
quiz.explanation: Side AB lies between ∠A and ∠B, so it is ASA.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a valid congruence rule?
quiz.explanation: SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) does not always give congruent triangles.

quiz.q: AB and CD bisect each other at O. Prove △AOC ≅ △BOD.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Since O is the midpoint of AB and CD: OA = OB and OC = OD.
∠AOC = ∠BOD (vertically opposite angles).
So two sides and the included angle are equal.
Hence △AOC ≅ △BOD by SAS.

quiz.q: Line l bisects ∠A, and B is a point on l. BP and BQ are perpendiculars from B to the arms of ∠A. Show that △APB ≅ △AQB and BP = BQ.
quiz.modelAnswer:
∠PAB = ∠QAB (l bisects ∠A).
∠APB = ∠AQB = 90°.
AB = AB (common).
So △APB ≅ △AQB by AAS.
Hence BP = BQ by CPCT.

topics.name: Isosceles Triangle Properties
topics.summary: Learn the theorems about equal sides and equal angles in a triangle.

steps.title: Isosceles triangle
steps.text: A triangle with two equal sides is called isosceles. The angles opposite those equal sides are called base angles.

steps.title: Theorem 1
steps.text: Angles opposite equal sides of a triangle are equal. We prove it by drawing the bisector of ∠A and using SAS.

steps.title: Theorem 2 (converse)
steps.text: Sides opposite equal angles of a triangle are equal. This is the converse of Theorem 1.

steps.title: Equilateral triangle
steps.text: If all three sides are equal, all three angles are equal. Since they add up to 180°, each angle is 60°.

steps.title: Using the property
steps.text: If you know one angle of an isosceles triangle, you can find the others using the angle sum property.

quiz.q: In △PQR, PQ = PR and ∠Q = 65°. What is ∠P?
Each angle of an equilateral triangle is:
quiz.explanation: Three equal angles add to 180°, so each is 60°.

quiz.q: In △ABC, ∠B = ∠C = 50°. Which sides are equal?
quiz.explanation: Sides opposite equal angles are equal: side opposite ∠C is AB and side opposite ∠B is AC.

quiz.q: In an isosceles triangle ABC with AB = AC, the vertex angle ∠A is 80°. Find ∠B and ∠C.
quiz.modelAnswer:
AB = AC, so ∠B = ∠C (angles opposite equal sides).
∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°.
80° + 2∠B = 180°, so 2∠B = 100°.
∠B = ∠C = 50°.

quiz.q: ABC is an isosceles triangle with AB = AC, and AD is the bisector of ∠A meeting BC at D. Show that AD bisects BC.
quiz.modelAnswer:
In △ABD and △ACD:
AB = AC (given), ∠BAD = ∠CAD (AD bisects ∠A), AD = AD (common).
So △ABD ≅ △ACD by SAS.
Hence BD = CD by CPCT, so AD bisects BC.

topics.name: SSS and RHS Congruence Rules
topics.summary: Prove triangles congruent using three sides, or using the hypotenuse and a side.

steps.title: SSS rule
steps.text: If all three sides of one triangle are equal to the three sides of another triangle, the two triangles are congruent.
steps.example: AB = PQ, BC = QR, CA = RP ⇒ △ABC ≅ △PQR (SSS)

steps.title: Right triangles
steps.text: In a right triangle, the side opposite the 90° angle is the hypotenuse. It is the longest side.

steps.title: RHS rule
steps.text: If the hypotenuse and one side of a right triangle are equal to the hypotenuse and one side of another right triangle, the two triangles are congruent.

steps.title: Choosing the right rule
steps.text: Mark what is given. Three sides → SSS. A right angle with hypotenuse and a side → RHS. Two sides with the angle between them → SAS. Two angles with a side → ASA or AAS.

quiz.q: What does the R in RHS stand for?
quiz.explanation: RHS = Right angle–Hypotenuse–Side.

quiz.q: Two triangles have sides 3, 4, 5 cm and 5, 3, 4 cm. They are congruent by:
quiz.explanation: All three sides match, so the rule is SSS.

quiz.q: RHS can be used only for:
quiz.explanation: RHS needs a right angle in both triangles.

quiz.q: AB is a line segment, and P and Q are points on opposite sides of AB such that PA = PB and QA = QB. Show that △PAQ ≅ △PBQ.
quiz.modelAnswer:
In △PAQ and △PBQ:
PA = PB (given)
QA = QB (given)
PQ = PQ (common)
So △PAQ ≅ △PBQ by SSS.

quiz.q: ABC is an isosceles triangle with AB = AC, and AD is perpendicular to BC. Prove that BD = CD.
quiz.modelAnswer:
In △ABD and △ACD:
∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90° (AD ⊥ BC)
Hypotenuse AB = AC (given)
AD = AD (common side)
So △ABD ≅ △ACD by RHS, and BD = CD by CPCT.

topics.name: Properties of a Parallelogram
topics.summary: Learn and prove the main properties of a parallelogram.

steps.title: What is a parallelogram?
steps.text: A quadrilateral whose two pairs of opposite sides are parallel. Rectangles, squares and rhombuses are special parallelograms.
steps.example: ABCD with AB ∥ DC and AD ∥ BC

steps.title: A diagonal splits it
steps.text: A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two congruent triangles. We prove it with ASA using alternate angles.

steps.title: Opposite sides and angles
steps.text: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal and opposite angles are equal.

steps.title: Diagonals bisect each other
steps.text: The diagonals of a parallelogram cut each other into two equal halves at their meeting point.
steps.example: If diagonals meet at O: OA = OC and OB = OD

steps.title: Adjacent angles
steps.text: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add up to 180°, because they are co-interior angles between parallel lines.

quiz.q: In parallelogram ABCD, ∠A = 75°. What is ∠C?
quiz.explanation: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.

quiz.q: The diagonals of a parallelogram always:
quiz.explanation: Only bisecting each other is true for every parallelogram.

quiz.q: Two adjacent angles of a parallelogram are in the ratio 2 : 3. The smaller angle is:
quiz.explanation: 2x + 3x = 180°, so x = 36° and the smaller angle is 72°.

quiz.q: Show that a diagonal of a parallelogram divides it into two congruent triangles.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Let ABCD be a parallelogram with diagonal AC.
AB ∥ DC with transversal AC, so ∠BAC = ∠DCA (alternate angles).
AD ∥ BC, so ∠BCA = ∠DAC (alternate angles).
AC = AC (common).
So △ABC ≅ △CDA by ASA.

quiz.q: The perimeter of a parallelogram is 40 cm and one side is 12 cm. Find the other sides.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Opposite sides are equal, so the sides are 12, x, 12, x.
Perimeter: 2(12 + x) = 40.
12 + x = 20, so x = 8 cm.
The sides are 12 cm, 8 cm, 12 cm and 8 cm.

topics.name: Conditions for a Parallelogram
topics.summary: Know which conditions are enough to show that a quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

steps.title: Converse theorems
steps.text: Each property has a converse. If a quadrilateral has that property, then it is a parallelogram.

steps.title: Opposite sides equal
steps.text: If both pairs of opposite sides of a quadrilateral are equal, it is a parallelogram.
steps.example: AB = CD and AD = BC ⇒ ABCD is a parallelogram

steps.title: Opposite angles equal
steps.text: If both pairs of opposite angles of a quadrilateral are equal, it is a parallelogram.

steps.title: Diagonals bisect each other
steps.text: If the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, it is a parallelogram.

steps.title: One pair equal and parallel
steps.text: If one pair of opposite sides is both equal and parallel, the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.
steps.example: AB = CD and AB ∥ CD ⇒ parallelogram

steps.title: Special cases
steps.text: A parallelogram with equal diagonals is a rectangle. One with perpendicular diagonals is a rhombus. One with both is a square.

quiz.q: A quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other is a:
quiz.explanation: Diagonals bisecting each other is enough for a parallelogram.

quiz.q: A parallelogram whose diagonals are equal is a:
quiz.explanation: Equal diagonals make a parallelogram a rectangle.

quiz.q: Which condition alone is enough for ABCD to be a parallelogram?
quiz.explanation: One pair of opposite sides must be both equal and parallel.

quiz.q: Show that if the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other at right angles, it is a rhombus.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Diagonals AC and BD bisect each other at O, so ABCD is a parallelogram.
In △AOB and △AOD: OB = OD, ∠AOB = ∠AOD = 90°, AO common.
So △AOB ≅ △AOD by SAS, and AB = AD by CPCT.
A parallelogram with equal adjacent sides has all sides equal, so ABCD is a rhombus.

quiz.q: In quadrilateral ABCD, ∠A = 110°, ∠C = 110°, ∠B = 70° and ∠D = 70°. Is ABCD a parallelogram? Give a reason.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Opposite angles: ∠A = ∠C = 110° and ∠B = ∠D = 70°.
Both pairs of opposite angles are equal.
Also the sum is 110 + 70 + 110 + 70 = 360°, which checks out.
So yes, ABCD is a parallelogram.

topics.name: The Mid-point Theorem
topics.summary: Use the mid-point theorem and its converse to solve problems.

steps.title: The theorem
steps.text: The line segment joining the mid-points of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side.
steps.example: E, F mid-points of AB, AC ⇒ EF ∥ BC

steps.title: Half the length
steps.text: That segment is also half the length of the third side.
steps.example: EF = ½ BC; if BC = 10 cm then EF = 5 cm

steps.title: Converse
steps.text: A line drawn through the mid-point of one side of a triangle, parallel to another side, bisects the third side.
steps.example: E is the mid-point of AB, line through E ∥ BC meets AC at F ⇒ AF = FC

steps.title: Joining all mid-points
steps.text: Joining the mid-points of the three sides makes four congruent triangles. Each is similar to the original, and the inner triangle has half its perimeter.

steps.title: Mid-points of a quadrilateral
steps.text: Joining the mid-points of the sides of any quadrilateral, in order, always gives a parallelogram.

quiz.q: In △ABC, D and E are mid-points of AB and AC. If BC = 14 cm, DE = ?
quiz.explanation: DE = ½ BC = 7 cm.

quiz.q: The figure formed by joining the mid-points of the sides of any quadrilateral in order is a:
quiz.explanation: By the mid-point theorem, opposite sides of that figure are parallel, so it is always a parallelogram.

quiz.q: A triangle has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 10 cm. The perimeter of the triangle formed by joining its mid-points is:
quiz.explanation: Each side is halved: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 cm.

quiz.q: ABCD is a rhombus and P, Q, R, S are the mid-points of AB, BC, CD and DA. Show that PQRS is a rectangle.
quiz.modelAnswer:
In △ABC, PQ ∥ AC and PQ = ½AC (mid-point theorem). Likewise SR ∥ AC and SR = ½AC.
So PQ = SR and PQ ∥ SR, and PQRS is a parallelogram.
Similarly PS ∥ BD.
The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular, so AC ⊥ BD, which gives PQ ⊥ PS.
A parallelogram with a right angle is a rectangle.

quiz.q: In △ABC, D is the mid-point of AB, and a line through D parallel to BC meets AC at E. If AC = 9 cm, find AE.
quiz.modelAnswer:
D is the mid-point of AB and DE ∥ BC.
By the converse of the mid-point theorem, E is the mid-point of AC.
So AE = ½ × AC = ½ × 9 = 4.5 cm.

topics.name: Chords and Angles at the Centre
topics.summary: Learn how equal chords and equal angles at the centre are related.

steps.title: Parts of a circle
steps.text: A chord joins two points on a circle. The longest chord is the diameter, which passes through the centre. A part of the circle between two points is an arc.

steps.title: Angle subtended by a chord
steps.text: Join the ends of a chord to the centre O. The angle formed at O is the angle subtended by the chord at the centre.
steps.example: Chord AB subtends ∠AOB at the centre

steps.title: Equal chords ⇒ equal angles
steps.text: Equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre. The proof uses SSS, since all radii are equal.

steps.title: Converse
steps.text: If two chords subtend equal angles at the centre, the chords are equal. This is proved using SAS.

steps.title: Same for congruent circles
steps.text: These results also hold for equal chords in two congruent circles (circles with equal radii).

quiz.q: The longest chord of a circle is the:
quiz.explanation: The diameter passes through the centre and is the longest chord.

quiz.q: Chords AB and CD of a circle are equal and ∠AOB = 70°. Then ∠COD =
quiz.explanation: Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre.

quiz.q: Equal chords subtending equal angles at the centre is proved with:
quiz.explanation: OA = OC, OB = OD (radii) and AB = CD (given) gives SSS.

quiz.q: Prove that equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Let AB = CD be chords of a circle with centre O.
In △AOB and △COD: OA = OC (radii), OB = OD (radii), AB = CD (given).
So △AOB ≅ △COD by SSS.
Hence ∠AOB = ∠COD by CPCT.

quiz.q: A chord of a circle equals its radius. Find the angle it subtends at the centre.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Let chord AB = radius r with centre O.
Then OA = OB = AB = r, so △OAB is equilateral.
Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°.
So ∠AOB = 60°.

topics.name: Perpendicular from the Centre to a Chord
topics.summary: Use perpendiculars from the centre to find chord lengths and distances.

steps.title: Perpendicular bisects the chord
steps.text: The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.

steps.title: Converse
steps.text: The line from the centre to the mid-point of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.
steps.example: M mid-point of AB ⇒ OM ⊥ AB

steps.title: Using Pythagoras
steps.text: The radius, half the chord and the distance from the centre make a right triangle.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.text: Radius 5 cm, chord 8 cm. Half the chord is 4 cm, so d² = 25 − 16 = 9 and d = 3 cm.

steps.title: Equal chords, equal distances
steps.text: Equal chords are equidistant from the centre. Chords equidistant from the centre are equal. A longer chord lies closer to the centre.

quiz.q: A chord of length 24 cm is in a circle of radius 13 cm. Its distance from the centre is:
The perpendicular from the centre to a chord:
quiz.explanation: It always cuts the chord into two equal parts.

quiz.q: Of two chords in a circle, the one nearer to the centre is:
quiz.explanation: Chords closer to the centre are longer, and the diameter is closest of all.

quiz.q: A chord is 3 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. Find the length of the chord.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Let OM ⊥ AB with OM = 3 cm and OA = 5 cm.
In right △OMA: AM² = OA² − OM² = 25 − 9 = 16, so AM = 4 cm.
The perpendicular bisects the chord, so AB = 2 × 4 = 8 cm.

quiz.q: Two parallel chords AB = 6 cm and CD = 8 cm lie on the same side of the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. Find the distance between them.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Distance of AB from O = √(5² − 3²) = √16 = 4 cm.
Distance of CD from O = √(5² − 4²) = √9 = 3 cm.
Both chords are on the same side of the centre.
Distance between them = 4 − 3 = 1 cm.

topics.name: Angle Subtended by an Arc
topics.summary: Relate the angle at the centre to angles on the circle.

steps.title: Centre angle vs circle angle
steps.text: An arc makes an angle at the centre, and also at any point on the remaining part of the circle.

steps.title: Double angle theorem
steps.text: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle it subtends at any point on the remaining part of the circle.

steps.title: Angles in the same segment
steps.text: Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal, because each is half of the same angle at the centre.
steps.example: ∠ACB = ∠ADB when C, D are on the same arc

steps.title: Angle in a semicircle
steps.text: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle. The diameter subtends 180° at the centre, so 90° on the circle.

steps.title: Concyclic points
steps.text: If the line joining two points subtends equal angles at two other points on the same side of it, all four points lie on one circle.

quiz.q: An arc subtends 120° at the centre. What angle does it subtend at a point on the remaining part of the circle?
quiz.explanation: The angle on the circle is half the angle at the centre.

quiz.q: The angle in a semicircle is:
quiz.explanation: The diameter subtends 180° at the centre, so 90° on the circle.

quiz.q: In a circle, ∠ACB = 35° and ∠ADB is in the same segment. ∠ADB =
quiz.explanation: Angles in the same segment are equal.

quiz.q: In a circle with centre O, ∠AOB = 140°. C is a point on the major arc. Find ∠ACB and ∠OAB.
quiz.modelAnswer:
∠ACB = ½ × ∠AOB = ½ × 140° = 70°.
In △OAB, OA = OB (radii), so ∠OAB = ∠OBA.
∠OAB = (180° − 140°)/2 = 20°.

quiz.q: AB is a diameter of a circle and C is a point on the circle with ∠CAB = 30°. Find ∠ABC.
quiz.modelAnswer:
AB is a diameter, so ∠ACB = 90° (angle in a semicircle).
In △ABC: ∠ABC = 180° − 90° − 30° = 60°.

topics.name: Cyclic Quadrilaterals
topics.summary: Learn the angle property of quadrilaterals drawn inside a circle.

steps.title: What is cyclic?
steps.text: A quadrilateral is cyclic if all four of its vertices lie on one circle.

steps.title: Opposite angles sum to 180°
steps.text: The sum of either pair of opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral is 180°. Each is half of angles at the centre that add to 360°.

steps.title: Converse
steps.text: If the sum of a pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral is 180°, the quadrilateral is cyclic.

steps.title: Exterior angle
steps.text: An exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle.

steps.title: Quick example
steps.text: In cyclic ABCD, ∠A = 70° and ∠B = 95°. Then ∠C = 110° and ∠D = 85°.

quiz.q: In cyclic quadrilateral PQRS, ∠P = 80°. ∠R =
quiz.explanation: Opposite angles add to 180°: 180° − 80° = 100°.

quiz.q: Which of these is always cyclic?
quiz.explanation: In a rectangle opposite angles are 90° + 90° = 180°.

quiz.q: In cyclic ABCD, side BC is extended to E and ∠DCE = 75°. Then ∠A =
quiz.explanation: The exterior angle equals the interior opposite angle.

quiz.q: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with ∠DBC = 70° and ∠BAC = 30°. Find ∠BCD.
quiz.modelAnswer:
∠BAC and ∠BDC are angles in the same segment, so ∠BDC = 30°.
Also ∠BAD = ∠BAC + ∠CAD, and ∠CAD = ∠CBD = 70° (same segment).
So ∠BAD = 30° + 70° = 100°.
∠BCD = 180° − 100° = 80° (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral).

quiz.q: Prove that a cyclic parallelogram is a rectangle.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Let ABCD be a cyclic parallelogram.
Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal: ∠A = ∠C.
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up: ∠A + ∠C = 180°.
So 2∠A = 180° and ∠A = 90°.
A parallelogram with one right angle is a rectangle.

topics.name: Area of a Triangle: Basics
topics.summary: Revise the area of a triangle using base and height.

steps.title: Base × height
steps.text: The basic formula is area = ½ × base × height. The height is the perpendicular from the opposite vertex to the base.

steps.title: Right triangle
steps.text: In a right triangle, the two sides around the right angle can be used as base and height.
steps.example: Legs 6 cm and 8 cm ⇒ area = ½ × 6 × 8 = 24 cm²

steps.title: Equilateral triangle
steps.text: For an equilateral triangle of side a, the area is (√3/4)a².

steps.title: The problem
steps.text: Often only the three sides are known and the height isn't. Finding the height is hard, so we need a formula that uses only the sides.

quiz.q: The area of a triangle with base 10 cm and height 6 cm is:
The area of an equilateral triangle with side 4 cm is:
A right triangle has legs 5 cm and 12 cm. Its area is:
Find the area of an equilateral triangle with side 6 cm.
The area of a triangle is 48 cm² and its base is 12 cm. Find its height.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Area = ½ × base × height.
48 = ½ × 12 × h
48 = 6h, so h = 8 cm.

topics.name: Heron's Formula
topics.summary: Find the area of any triangle from its three sides.

steps.title: Semi-perimeter
steps.text: First find the semi-perimeter s, which is half of the perimeter.

steps.title: The formula
steps.text: Heron's formula gives the area from the sides a, b and c.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.text: Sides 3, 4 and 5 cm: s = 6, so area = √(6 × 3 × 2 × 1) = √36 = 6 cm².

steps.title: Tips
steps.text: Check that s − a, s − b and s − c are all positive. Factorise the numbers under the root to simplify, for example 7056 = 84².

quiz.q: The semi-perimeter of a triangle with sides 7, 8 and 9 cm is:
The area of a triangle with sides 5, 5 and 6 cm is:
In Heron's formula, s stands for:
quiz.explanation: s is half the perimeter.

quiz.q: Find the area of a triangle with sides 18 cm, 24 cm and 30 cm.
An isosceles triangle has perimeter 18 cm and each equal side is 5 cm. Find its area.

topics.name: Applications of Heron's Formula
topics.summary: Solve real-life area problems using Heron's formula.

steps.title: Real-life triangles
steps.text: Triangular parks, signboards, walls and fields often have known side lengths but unknown heights. Heron's formula is perfect for these.

steps.title: Sides in a ratio
steps.text: If sides are in a ratio like 12 : 17 : 25 and the perimeter is given, write the sides as 12x, 17x, 25x and solve for x first.

steps.title: Finding cost
steps.text: Find the area first, then multiply by the rate.

steps.title: Finding a height
steps.text: Once you know the area, you can find any height using area = ½ × base × height.

quiz.q: A triangular park has sides 6 m, 8 m and 10 m. Its area is:
A triangle has area 84 cm² and longest side 15 cm. The height on that side is:
A triangular field has area 120 m². Painting costs ₹5 per m². The total cost is:
The sides of a triangular plot are in the ratio 3 : 5 : 7 and its perimeter is 300 m. Find its area.
A triangular signboard has sides 8 cm, 11 cm and perimeter 32 cm. Find its area.

topics.name: Surface Area of a Right Circular Cone
topics.summary: Find the curved and total surface area of a cone.

steps.title: Parts of a cone
steps.text: A right circular cone has a circular base of radius r, a height h from the vertex to the centre of the base, and a slant height l along its side.

steps.title: Slant height
steps.text: The radius, height and slant height form a right triangle.

steps.title: Curved surface area
steps.text: If you open up the curved surface of a cone, it becomes a sector of a circle.

steps.title: Total surface area
steps.text: Add the area of the circular base to the curved surface area.

quiz.q: The slant height of a cone with r = 6 cm and h = 8 cm is:
The curved surface area of a cone is:
quiz.explanation: CSA = πrl; πr(l + r) is the total surface area.

quiz.q: The CSA of a cone with r = 7 cm and l = 10 cm (π = 22/7) is:
Find the total surface area of a cone with radius 21 m and slant height 29 m. (π = 22/7)
A conical tent is 10 m high and its base radius is 24 m. Find its slant height and the canvas needed (curved surface only). Use π = 3.14.

topics.name: Surface Area of a Sphere and Hemisphere
topics.summary: Find the surface areas of spheres and hemispheres.

steps.title: Sphere
steps.text: A sphere is a perfectly round 3D shape, like a ball. Every point on it is the same distance r from the centre.

steps.title: Surface area of a sphere
steps.text: The surface area of a sphere is four times the area of a circle with the same radius.

steps.title: Hemisphere
steps.text: A hemisphere is half a sphere. Its curved surface is half the sphere's surface.

steps.title: Total surface area of a hemisphere
steps.text: A solid hemisphere also has a flat circular face, so we add πr².

steps.title: Example
steps.text: r = 7 cm: sphere SA = 4 × (22/7) × 49 = 616 cm². Hemisphere CSA = 308 cm², TSA = 462 cm².

quiz.q: The surface area of a sphere of radius 3.5 cm (π = 22/7) is:
The total surface area of a solid hemisphere is:
quiz.explanation: Curved surface 2πr² plus flat base πr² gives 3πr².

quiz.q: If the radius of a sphere is doubled, its surface area becomes:
quiz.explanation: SA ∝ r², so (2)² = 4 times.

quiz.q: Find the ratio of the surface areas of two spheres with radii 2 cm and 3 cm.
quiz.modelAnswer:
SA₁ = 4π(2)² = 16π and SA₂ = 4π(3)² = 36π.
Ratio = 16π : 36π = 4 : 9.

quiz.q: A hemispherical bowl has inner radius 10.5 cm. Find the cost of tin-plating the inside at ₹16 per 100 cm². (π = 22/7)

topics.name: Volume of a Right Circular Cone
topics.summary: Find how much space a cone holds.

steps.title: Volume means capacity
steps.text: Volume is the space a solid takes up. It is measured in cubic units such as cm³ or m³. 1 litre = 1000 cm³.

steps.title: Cone vs cylinder
steps.text: A cone fills exactly one-third of a cylinder with the same base and height.

steps.title: Formula
steps.text: The volume of a cone is one-third of π times the radius squared times the height.

steps.title: Finding h from l
steps.text: If only the slant height is given, find the height first using h = √(l² − r²).

quiz.q: The volume of a cone is:
quiz.explanation: A cone holds one-third of a cylinder with the same base and height.

quiz.q: The volume of a cone with r = 3 cm and h = 7 cm (π = 22/7) is:
A cone and a cylinder have the same base and height. The ratio of their volumes is:
quiz.explanation: V(cone) : V(cylinder) = ⅓ : 1 = 1 : 3.

quiz.q: Find the volume of a cone with radius 6 cm and slant height 10 cm. (Leave the answer in terms of π.)
A conical pit has top diameter 3.5 m and depth 12 m. Find its capacity in kilolitres. (π = 22/7)

topics.name: Volume of a Sphere and Hemisphere
topics.summary: Find the volume of balls, domes and bowls.

steps.title: Volume of a sphere
steps.text: The volume of a sphere of radius r is four-thirds π times r cubed.

steps.title: Volume of a hemisphere
steps.text: A hemisphere is half a sphere, so its volume is half.

steps.title: Scaling
steps.text: Volume depends on r³. If the radius is doubled, the volume becomes 2³ = 8 times.

steps.title: Capacity in litres
steps.text: To convert cm³ to litres, divide by 1000.

quiz.q: The volume of a sphere of radius 21 cm (π = 22/7) is:
The volume of a hemisphere is:
quiz.explanation: Half of (4/3)πr³ is (2/3)πr³.

quiz.q: If the radius of a ball is halved, its volume becomes:
quiz.explanation: (½)³ = ⅛.

quiz.q: Find the capacity in litres of a hemispherical bowl of radius 10.5 cm. (π = 22/7)
The diameter of the Moon is about one-fourth of the Earth's diameter. What fraction of the Earth's volume is the Moon's volume?
quiz.modelAnswer:
Let the Earth's radius be r. Then the Moon's radius is r/4.
V(Moon) = (4/3)π(r/4)³ = (1/64) × (4/3)πr³.
So the Moon's volume is 1/64 of the Earth's volume.

topics.name: Data and Frequency Tables
topics.summary: Organise raw data into grouped frequency tables.

steps.title: What is data?
steps.text: Data is a collection of facts or numbers, such as marks or heights. Raw data is data in its original, unorganised form.

steps.title: Frequency
steps.text: Frequency is how many times a value occurs. Tally marks (||||) help us count quickly.
steps.example: Marks 5 appear 4 times ⇒ frequency of 5 is 4

steps.title: Class intervals
steps.text: For large data, we group values into classes like 0–10 and 10–20. In 10–20, 10 is the lower limit and 20 is the upper limit.
steps.example: Class width (size) = upper limit − lower limit = 10

steps.title: Exclusive classes
steps.text: In classes like 10–20 and 20–30, the upper limit is not included. So 20 goes into 20–30.

steps.title: Class mark
steps.text: The class mark is the mid-point of a class.

quiz.q: The class mark of the class 30–40 is:
In the classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, the value 20 goes into:
quiz.explanation: The upper limit is excluded, so 20 belongs to 20–30.

quiz.q: The width of the class 15–25 is:
Find the class marks of the classes 10–25, 25–40 and 40–55, and state the class size.

topics.name: Bar Graphs
topics.summary: Draw and read bar graphs.

steps.title: What is a bar graph?
steps.text: A bar graph shows data using bars of equal width with equal gaps between them. The height (or length) of each bar shows the value.

steps.title: Axes
steps.text: Categories such as months or subjects go on one axis. Values go on the other axis, using a suitable scale.

steps.title: Drawing steps
steps.text: Draw the axes. Choose a scale. Mark the categories with equal gaps. Draw bars of equal width up to each value. Label the axes and give a title.

steps.title: Reading a bar graph
steps.text: The tallest bar shows the largest value and the shortest bar shows the smallest. You can compare bars, find differences, and find totals.

quiz.q: In a bar graph, the width of the bars is:
quiz.explanation: Bars have equal widths; only their heights show the values.

quiz.q: With the scale 1 cm = 20 units, a bar of 3.5 cm shows:
Gaps between the bars of a bar graph are:
quiz.explanation: A bar graph has equal gaps between bars.

quiz.q: Favourite sports of 40 students: Cricket 15, Football 10, Hockey 5, Badminton 10. Describe how to draw a bar graph and say which sport is most popular.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Put the sports on the x-axis and the number of students on the y-axis.
Use the scale 1 cm = 2 students.
Draw bars of equal width with equal gaps: Cricket 7.5 cm, Football 5 cm, Hockey 2.5 cm, Badminton 5 cm.
Cricket has the tallest bar, so it is the most popular.

quiz.q: A bar graph shows a shop's sales: Mon 40, Tue 55, Wed 30, Thu 65. Find the total sales and the difference between the highest and lowest days.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Total = 40 + 55 + 30 + 65 = 190.
Highest = Thu (65), lowest = Wed (30).
Difference = 65 − 30 = 35.

topics.name: Histograms and Frequency Polygons
topics.summary: Represent grouped data with histograms and frequency polygons.

steps.title: Histogram
steps.text: A histogram is like a bar graph for continuous class intervals. The bars touch each other with no gaps. Class intervals go on the x-axis and frequencies on the y-axis.

steps.title: Kink on the axis
steps.text: If the first class does not start at 0, draw a kink (zig-zag) on the x-axis near the origin to show a break in the scale.

steps.title: Unequal class widths
steps.text: If class widths differ, the bar heights must be adjusted so that the areas are proportional to the frequencies.
steps.example: Adjusted frequency = (minimum class width ÷ class width) × frequency

steps.title: Frequency polygon
steps.text: Join the mid-points of the tops of the histogram bars with straight lines. Add a class of zero frequency at each end to close the polygon.

steps.title: Without a histogram
steps.text: You can also draw a frequency polygon by plotting (class mark, frequency) points and joining them with line segments.

quiz.q: In a histogram, the bars:
quiz.explanation: Histograms use continuous classes, so the bars are adjacent.

quiz.q: A frequency polygon is drawn by joining:
options: Mid-points of the tops of the bars
quiz.explanation: We join the mid-points (class marks) at the frequency heights.

quiz.q: A class 20–40 has frequency 12 and the minimum class width is 10. Its adjusted frequency is:
Weekly wages in ₹: 500–600: 5, 600–700: 8, 700–800: 12, 800–900: 4. Explain how to draw a histogram and a frequency polygon.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Mark the classes on the x-axis with a kink near 0, and frequency on the y-axis.
Draw touching bars of heights 5, 8, 12 and 4.
Mark the class marks 550, 650, 750, 850 at those heights.
Add (450, 0) and (950, 0), then join all the points with straight lines.

quiz.q: Classes: 0–10 (f = 5), 10–30 (f = 16), 30–60 (f = 12). Find the adjusted heights for a histogram.

topics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
topics.summary: Break any composite number into primes and see why that breakup is unique.

steps.title: Primes and Composites
steps.text: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. A composite number has more than two factors. 1 is neither prime nor composite.

steps.title: Prime Factorisation
steps.text: Keep dividing a number by primes (a factor tree) until only primes are left. Write repeated primes using powers.

steps.title: The Theorem
steps.text: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every composite number can be written as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique, apart from the order of the primes.

steps.title: Using the Theorem
steps.text: A number ends in 0 only if it has both 2 and 5 as prime factors. Using uniqueness, we can prove some numbers can never end in 0.
steps.example: 4ⁿ = 2²ⁿ has no prime factor 5, so 4ⁿ never ends with 0

quiz.q: What is the prime factorisation of 140?
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says prime factorisation is unique except for:
quiz.explanation: Only the order can change; the primes and their powers are always the same.

quiz.q: For a natural number n, which of these can end with the digit 0?
quiz.explanation: 10ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 5ⁿ has both 2 and 5 as factors. The others have no factor 5.

quiz.q: Check whether 6ⁿ can end with the digit 0 for any natural number n.
quiz.modelAnswer:
6ⁿ = (2 × 3)ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ.
A number ending in 0 must be divisible by 10 = 2 × 5, so it needs the prime factor 5.
By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, the only primes in 6ⁿ are 2 and 3.
So 5 is not a factor of 6ⁿ.
Hence 6ⁿ can never end with the digit 0.

quiz.q: Express 5005 as a product of its prime factors.

topics.name: HCF and LCM using Primes
topics.summary: Find HCF and LCM by prime factorisation and use HCF × LCM = product.

steps.title: HCF from Primes
steps.text: Write each number as a product of primes. HCF is the product of the smallest power of each prime that is common to all the numbers.

steps.title: LCM from Primes
steps.text: LCM is the product of the greatest power of every prime that appears in any of the numbers.

steps.title: The Product Rule
steps.text: For any two positive integers a and b, HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b. Use it to find one value when the other three are known.

steps.title: Three Numbers
steps.text: For three numbers, find HCF and LCM the same way using primes. But the product rule does NOT work for three numbers.

quiz.q: What is the HCF of 96 and 404?
quiz.explanation: 96 = 2⁵ × 3 and 404 = 2² × 101. The common prime is 2 with smallest power 2², so HCF = 4.

quiz.q: What is the LCM of 12, 15 and 21?
The HCF of two numbers is 9 and their LCM is 459. If one number is 27, the other is:
Find the HCF and LCM of 96 and 404 by prime factorisation. Verify that HCF × LCM = product of the numbers.
Given that HCF(306, 657) = 9, find LCM(306, 657).
quiz.modelAnswer:
We know HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers.
LCM = (306 × 657) ÷ 9.
657 ÷ 9 = 73, so LCM = 306 × 73.
LCM = 22338.

topics.name: Proving Numbers Irrational
topics.summary: Prove that numbers like √2, √5 and 3 + 2√5 are irrational.

steps.title: What is Irrational?
steps.text: A number is irrational if it cannot be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Their decimals never end and never repeat.

steps.title: A Key Fact
steps.text: Let p be a prime. If p divides a², then p also divides a. This comes from the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic and is used in every proof.
steps.example: If 2 divides a², then 2 divides a

steps.title: Proof by Contradiction: √2
steps.text: Assume √2 = a/b with a, b co-prime. Then 2b² = a², so 2 divides a. Put a = 2c: b² = 2c², so 2 divides b. Now 2 divides both a and b, a contradiction. So √2 is irrational.

steps.title: Sums and Products
steps.text: Rational + irrational is irrational. A non-zero rational × irrational is irrational. Use this, again by contradiction, for numbers like 5 − √3 or 3√2.
steps.example: If 5 − √3 = a/b, then √3 = 5 − a/b would be rational — impossible

quiz.q: Which of these is irrational?
quiz.explanation: √16 = 4, 0.25 = 1/4 and 22/7 are rational. 7 is not a perfect square, so √7 is irrational.

quiz.q: The proof that √3 is irrational uses the method of:
quiz.explanation: We assume √3 is rational and reach a contradiction.

quiz.q: The number (2 + √3)(2 − √3) is:
quiz.explanation: (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 4 − 3 = 1, which is rational. A product of two irrationals can be rational.

quiz.q: Prove that √5 is irrational.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Assume √5 is rational, so √5 = a/b where a, b are co-prime integers, b ≠ 0.
Then 5b² = a², so 5 divides a², hence 5 divides a.
Let a = 5c. Then 5b² = 25c², so b² = 5c².
So 5 divides b², hence 5 divides b.
Now 5 divides both a and b, which contradicts that they are co-prime.
Hence √5 is irrational.

quiz.q: Given that √5 is irrational, prove that 3 + 2√5 is irrational.
quiz.modelAnswer:
Assume 3 + 2√5 is rational, so 3 + 2√5 = a/b, with a, b integers, b ≠ 0.
Then 2√5 = a/b − 3, so √5 = (a − 3b)/(2b).
Since a and b are integers, (a − 3b)/(2b) is rational.
So √5 would be rational, which contradicts the fact that √5 is irrational.
Hence 3 + 2√5 is irrational.

topics.name: Polynomials and Their Zeroes
topics.summary: Know the types of polynomials, find their values and their zeroes.

steps.title: Degree
steps.text: A polynomial in x has whole-number powers of x. The highest power of x is its degree.

steps.title: Types
steps.text: Degree 1 is linear (ax + b), degree 2 is quadratic (ax² + bx + c), degree 3 is cubic (ax³ + bx² + cx + d), with a ≠ 0.

steps.title: Value of a Polynomial
steps.text: To find p(k), replace x by k in p(x) and simplify.

steps.title: Zeroes
steps.text: If p(k) = 0, then k is a zero of p(x). A linear polynomial ax + b has exactly one zero, x = −b/a.

quiz.q: What is the degree of 5x³ − 4x² + x − 2?
quiz.explanation: The highest power of x is 3.

quiz.q: The zero of 2x + 3 is:
quiz.explanation: 2x + 3 = 0 gives x = −3/2. Remember the sign: zero = −b/a.

quiz.q: Which of these is a quadratic polynomial?
quiz.explanation: Its highest power is 2. √x + 1 is not a polynomial since the power ½ is not a whole number.

quiz.q: Check whether −1 and 4 are zeroes of p(x) = x² − 3x − 4.
quiz.modelAnswer:
p(−1) = (−1)² − 3(−1) − 4 = 1 + 3 − 4 = 0.
p(4) = 4² − 3(4) − 4 = 16 − 12 − 4 = 0.
Since both values are 0, −1 and 4 are zeroes of p(x).

quiz.q: Find the value of p(x) = x³ − 2x² + x − 5 at x = 2.

topics.name: Geometrical Meaning of Zeroes
topics.summary: See zeroes as the points where a polynomial's graph meets the x-axis.

steps.title: Linear Graphs
steps.text: The graph of y = ax + b is a straight line. It cuts the x-axis at exactly one point, (−b/a, 0). So a linear polynomial has one zero.

steps.title: Quadratic Graphs
steps.text: The graph of y = ax² + bx + c is a U-shaped curve called a parabola. It opens upward if a > 0 and downward if a < 0.

steps.title: Counting Zeroes on a Graph
steps.text: The zeroes are the x-coordinates of the points where the graph meets the x-axis. A quadratic can meet it at 2, 1 or 0 points.
steps.example: y = x² − 4 meets at x = −2 and x = 2

steps.title: Higher Degrees
steps.text: A cubic polynomial has at most 3 zeroes. In general, a polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes.

quiz.q: The graph of y = x² − 4 meets the x-axis at:
quiz.explanation: x² − 4 = 0 gives x = ±2. (0, −4) is where it meets the y-axis.

quiz.q: The graph of y = p(x) touches the x-axis at exactly one point. The number of zeroes of p(x) is:
quiz.explanation: Each meeting point with the x-axis gives one zero.

quiz.q: The maximum number of zeroes a cubic polynomial can have is:
quiz.explanation: A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes.

quiz.q: The graph of y = p(x) meets the x-axis only at x = −2, x = 1 and x = 3. How many zeroes does p(x) have? Name them and state the least possible degree of p(x).
quiz.modelAnswer:
Zeroes are the x-coordinates where the graph meets the x-axis.
The graph meets it at 3 points, so p(x) has 3 zeroes.
The zeroes are −2, 1 and 3.
A polynomial with 3 zeroes must have degree at least 3, so the least degree is 3 (cubic).

quiz.q: Explain why the polynomial x² + 1 has no real zeroes, using its graph.
quiz.modelAnswer:
For every real x, x² ≥ 0, so x² + 1 ≥ 1 > 0.
So y = x² + 1 is always positive.
Its graph is a parabola opening upward with lowest point (0, 1), lying above the x-axis.
It never meets the x-axis, so x² + 1 has no real zeroes.

topics.name: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic
topics.summary: Link the sum and product of zeroes to the coefficients, and build quadratics.

steps.title: The Two Rules
steps.text: If α and β are the zeroes of ax² + bx + c, then sum α + β = −b/a and product αβ = c/a.
